newsitem.title: USA: El Nino could bring droughts to S. Africa, Australia.
newsitem.headline: El Nino could bring droughts to S. Africa, Australia.

text.p: A strong "El Nino" weather pattern in the tropical Pacific could trigger cool, wet weather in the U.S. South next winter and bring drought to South Africa, Australia and parts of Brazil, scientists said on Tuesday.

El Nino has already triggered a drought in India this summer, as evidenced by the weak start to that country's annual monsoon, Ants Leetmaa, director of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Centre, said.

"This is a big event," he added, referring to the size of the latest El Nino, a warm ocean temperature phenomenon that occurs approximately every two to seven years with profound consequences for global weather.
Leetma added his personal prediction that the Southeast United States would experience hot, dry conditions this summer.

But in general, scientists at the Climate Prediction Centre said they could not accurately predict summer weather based on the presence of an El Nino because not enough is known yet about the links between the two.

In addition to the wetter, cooler weather expected in the U.S. South from November through March, the northern United States from Washington to the Great Lakes will be warmer than normal over the same period, Leetmaa said.

But in Australia, he said "we anticipate the dryness we're seeing is going to develop into a full-scale drought" during its summer season in November through March, when the Australian monsoon normally appears.
Drought conditions are also expected in northeastern Brazil and South Africa during the same time period, Leetma said.

Meanwhile, "record-breaking floods" now occuring in Northern Chile and stretching across to the other side of South America indicate the type of weather that could develop in the U.S. South next winter, he said.
El Nino also is associated with flooding in the Midwest, the most dramatic example being the huge Mississippi River floods of 1993, Leetmaa said.
"We certainly don't anticipate, at this stage,... anything like the 1993 flooding," Leetma said.
But there is "some suggestion" that above-normal precipitation could occur in areas, such Texas up to the Pacific Northwest, where below-normal temperatures are expected next winter, he said.
